# Results — Study 913 (Tracking-Difference Persistence) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Each fund's **tracking
difference** (TD) is its complete-calendar-year total return minus a common family proxy
(the cross-sectional mean of the family — the ranking is invariant to that choice). We test
whether last year's TD rank predicts next year's, then race five annually-rebalanced rules:
`winner` (last year's best TD), `loser`, `cheapest` (lowest published expense ratio, never
traded), `leader` (the flagship, never traded) and `eqw`. Exactly one execution lag — the
ranking uses returns through the last close of year `y` and the weights are in force from
the **second** trading day of year `y+1`. Costs are 1 bp one-way × NAV on realised
turnover; there is no short leg, so no borrow. Daily **total-return** closes (`yfinance`,
`auto_adjust=True`). As-of **2026-06-30**; partial calendar years are dropped at both ends.*

## Data stamp

| Family | Members (leader first) | Window | n days | Complete years | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|--:|--:|---|
| S&P 500 ETF trio | SPY, IVV, VOO | 2010-09-09 → 2026-06-30 | 3,975 | 2011–2025 (15) | `f11699949902` |
| S&P 500 full ladder | + VFIAX, FXAIX, SWPPX | 2011-05-04 → 2026-06-30 | 3,811 | 2012–2025 (14) | `82068f45e436` |
| Nasdaq-100 pair | QQQ, QQQM | 2020-10-13 → 2026-06-30 | 1,434 | 2021–2025 (5) | `b33e0709c240` |

**SPLG is missing, not omitted.** The requested tape named SPLG (the 2 bp SPDR Portfolio
S&P 500 ETF). At build time Yahoo! Finance returns a **single stale bar** for it
(2026-07-17) and refuses every historical range — a broken source record. It is declared
`data.UNAVAILABLE` rather than quietly swapped for something else.

**Non-tape inputs (ASSUMPTIONS, both swept below).** (i) Expense ratios, taken from issuer
disclosure at build time: SPY 9.45, IVV 3.0, VOO 3.0, VFIAX 4.0, FXAIX 1.5, SWPPX 2.0,
QQQ 20.0, QQQM 15.0 bp/yr. Several were cut during the sample (IVV 7→3, SWPPX 9→2 in 2017,
FXAIX 1.5 only since 2019), so the ladder is a level, not a history — **and applying today's
level to 2012 is hindsight in the `cheapest` rule's fund choice.** That is priced explicitly
in *Hindsight in the fee sheet* below, not waved away. (ii) The capital-gains rate and
embedded gain in the tax break-even.

**Price-only vs total-return.** Everything above is total return. The one price-only series
in the study is ^GSPC, kept precisely to show what it *cannot* do: measured against it, all
six S&P 500 funds show a TD of **+201 to +211 bp/yr**, which is the dividend yield, not a
tracking difference. The *level* of TD is not identified from a public tape; only
cross-fund differences within a family are.

## The measurement — relative TD in basis points

S&P 500 ETF trio (relative to the family mean; each row sums to zero):

| year | SPY | IVV | VOO | | year | SPY | IVV | VOO |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2011 | +0.5 | −1.2 | +0.7 | | 2019 | −5.6 | −2.8 | +8.5 |
| 2012 | −2.3 | +4.4 | −2.1 | | 2020 | −2.0 | +4.6 | −2.7 |
| 2013 | −2.6 | −2.7 | +5.3 | | 2021 | −3.2 | −0.2 | +3.4 |
| 2014 | +14.4 | +24.8 | **−39.2** | | 2022 | −0.5 | +0.9 | −0.4 |
| 2015 | −4.7 | +0.3 | +4.4 | | 2023 | −9.3 | +3.7 | +5.5 |
| 2016 | +9.6 | **−36.1** | +26.5 | | 2024 | −4.6 | +0.2 | +4.4 |
| 2017 | −3.9 | +1.0 | +2.9 | | 2025 | −7.7 | +5.0 | +2.7 |
| 2018 | −4.9 | +3.0 | +1.9 | | | | | |

**The noise floor is the story.** The standard deviation of relative TD is **10.7 bp** in
the trio and **9.7 bp** in the full ladder — larger than the 6.45 bp fee spread the trio
actually contains. The two bolded years (VOO 2014, IVV 2016) are dividend-timing artefacts
of the adjusted close, not 40 bp of real slippage, and they fully reverse the next year.
This is the study's central measurement caveat, and it has a precise form: **in any single
year** no family here is resolvable (trio 6.45 bp of fee against a 10.7 bp sd; ladder 7.95
against 9.7; pair 5.0 against 5.0). Only the sample *mean* resolves it — sd/√years is 2.8,
2.6 and 2.2 bp respectively — which is exactly why a rule reading last year's ranking
fails while a rule reading the fee sheet does not need to estimate anything at all.

## Does the TD rank persist?

| Family | mean YoY Spearman | *t* | pairs | permutation *p* | residual (fund-demeaned) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| S&P 500 ETF trio | **+0.071** | +0.43 | 14 | 0.964 | −0.179 (*t* = −0.92) |
| S&P 500 full ladder | **+0.253** | +2.34 | 13 | 0.307 | +0.200 (*t* = +1.71) |
| Nasdaq-100 pair | +1.000 (degenerate) | — | 4 | 1.000 | 0.000 |

Three readings, and they fit together:

- **Inside the ETF trio there is no persistence at all** (+0.07, *t* = 0.43, permutation
  *p* = 0.96). SPY is 6.45 bp dearer than IVV/VOO, and 6.45 bp does not clear a 10.7 bp
  noise floor in a single year.
- **Across the full ladder persistence appears** (+0.25, *t* = +2.34) — but the permutation
  test says it is **not a year-to-year memory**. Shuffling the order of the calendar years
  reproduces it (*p* = 0.31), because the mean rank correlation over **all** year pairs
  (+0.195) is essentially the consecutive-pair figure (+0.253). What persists is a
  *time-invariant level*: the published fee ordering, visible from any year to any other.
- **The Nasdaq pair is the same fact in its purest form.** QQQM (15 bp) out-returns QQQ
  (20 bp) in **5 of 5** complete years by 2.8 to 15.6 bp (mean **+8.55 bp/yr**, *t* = +3.95,
  bootstrap CI [+4.7, +12.5]). With two funds Spearman degenerates to a sign indicator, so
  the *persistence* reading is a 4/4 sign run over consecutive pairs, not an independent rank
  test — and five years is five years.

## The money question — the rules, at 1 bp one-way

*t* (annual) is the paired *t* on the per-year gap; *t* (HAC) is Newey-West with one annual
lag on the same series — calendar years do not overlap, so the two agree closely, and the
HAC figure is shown so that independence is never simply assumed.

| Family | winner − cheapest | cheapest − leader | winner − leader |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| S&P 500 ETF trio (14 live yrs) | **+0.33** bp/yr, *t* = +0.10 (HAC +0.10), 7/14 yrs + | +3.27 bp/yr, *t* = +1.26 (HAC +1.40), 12/14 + | +3.60, *t* = +0.77 |
| S&P 500 full ladder (13 live yrs) | **−6.08** bp/yr, *t* = −1.03 (HAC −1.22), 3/13 yrs + | **+10.64** bp/yr, ***t* = +4.85** (HAC +4.78), 11/13 + | +4.57, *t* = +0.83 |
| Nasdaq-100 pair (4 live yrs) | **0.00** (the winner *is* the cheapest) | **+8.79** bp/yr, ***t* = +2.93** (HAC +4.32), 4/4 + | +8.79, *t* = +2.93 |

Block-bootstrap 95% CIs on the annual gap (5,000 draws, 2-year blocks): winner − cheapest
[−5.9, +6.6] (trio) and [−17.4, +0.9] (ladder) — both straddle or sit below zero;
cheapest − leader [+6.1, +14.8] (ladder) and [+4.5, +13.1] (pair) — both clear of zero.

The rule window is one year shorter than the measurement window everywhere, because the
first complete year is consumed by the ranking: the pair's **5/5** raw-TD run is **4/4** once
it has to be traded, and the *t* = +2.93 is computed on those four years, not five.

The `winner` rule changed fund **10 times in 14 live years** (trio) and 8 times in 13
(ladder) to buy exactly nothing. The `cheapest` and `leader` rules never switch fund. One
disclosure there: where `cheapest` is a **tie** (the trio's IVV/VOO at 3 bp) it is held at a
constant 50/50 target, i.e. implicitly rebalanced daily and charged nothing for it. On funds
this similar the freebie is **+0.06 bp/yr** — immaterial at this resolution, but it means
only the single-fund arms are literally buy-and-hold.

**Daily vs annual unit.** The HAC *t* on the *daily* return difference is +0.03 / −0.89 /
+0.28 — near zero everywhere, including for the gaps that are strongly significant
annually. That is not a contradiction: the daily cross-fund difference is dominated by
same-day print and dividend-timing noise that reverses within days, so the daily test has
almost no power against a quantity that is defined once a year. Both are reported; the
annual figure is the one that carries meaning, and the daily one is the honest conservative
floor.

**Sharpe is blind to all of it.** Excess-of-cash Sharpe (vs BIL, both arms excess), trio:
winner 0.8230, cheapest 0.8228, leader 0.8241, eqw 0.8234 — the arms share ~99.99% of their
variance, so a real 3–11 bp/yr edge is invisible in the fourth decimal of a Sharpe ratio.
A tracking-difference edge can only be read as a return *gap*.

## Hindsight in the fee sheet — the selection-free control

The `cheapest` arm is the one place a look-ahead can enter this study, and it does. Nothing
in the *return* series peeks — the ranking is acted on one trading day after the year it is
formed — but the fund `cheapest` holds is chosen from the fee sheet published **today**, and
FXAIX has only charged 1.5 bp since 2019 (SWPPX 2 bp since 2017, IVV 3 bp since 2016). An
investor in 2012 knew SPY was the dearest; they did not know which low-fee rung would end up
lowest. So the headline +10.64 bp/yr is, in substance, *FXAIX chosen ex post*.

The control removes the choice: race **every** non-flagship fund against the flagship, plus
the equal-weight blend of all of them — a rule that needs no fee sheet, no ranking, and no
forecast (`strategy.per_fund_gap_vs_leader`, buy-and-hold, no costs to charge).

| vs the flagship | S&P 500 full ladder (14 yrs) | | Nasdaq-100 (5 yrs) |
|---|--:|---|--:|
| IVV − SPY | +2.37 bp/yr, *t* = +0.62, 12/14 + | QQQM − QQQ | **+8.55** bp/yr, *t* = +3.95, 5/5 + |
| VOO − SPY | +3.46 bp/yr, *t* = +0.75, 12/14 + | | CI [+4.7, +12.5] |
| SWPPX − SPY | +4.47 bp/yr, *t* = +1.59, 10/14 + | | |
| VFIAX − SPY | +6.04 bp/yr, *t* = +2.49, 10/14 + | | |
| FXAIX − SPY | **+9.71** bp/yr, *t* = +4.38, 11/14 + | | |
| **equal weight of all five** | **+5.21** bp/yr, ***t* = +2.68** (HAC +2.77), 11/14 +, CI [+1.8, +8.8] | | |

Three readings, and the middle one is the honest headline:

1. **Every** non-flagship fund beats SPY, so the *sign* owes nothing to hindsight — SPY has
   been the dearest of its family throughout, and that much was public in advance.
2. The **hindsight-free magnitude is +5.21 bp/yr (*t* = +2.68)**, roughly **half** the
   +10.64 the fee-sheet rule reports. Half the headline is the fund pick.
3. The spread across rows (+2.4 to +9.7) is the size of the selection problem. The two ETFs
   that were *already* cheap in 2012 (IVV, VOO) deliver a gap that does not clear *t* = 1.

The Nasdaq pair has no selection to make — two funds, one obviously dearer — and it is the
cleaner reading of the same fact, at the cost of only five years.

## Robustness — eras

| Family / gap | early | late |
|---|--:|--:|
| Trio, cheapest − leader | 2012–2018: −0.55 bp/yr, *t* = −0.12, 5/7 + | 2019–2025: **+7.09** bp/yr, *t* = **+4.02**, 7/7 + |
| Ladder, cheapest − leader | 2013–2018: +10.94 bp/yr, *t* = +3.52, 5/6 + | 2019–2025: +10.39 bp/yr, *t* = +3.14, 6/7 + |
| Pair, cheapest − leader | 2022–2023: +8.41 bp/yr, 2/2 + | 2024–2025: +9.16 bp/yr, 2/2 + |
| Ladder, winner − cheapest | 2013–2018: −11.35 bp/yr, *t* = −0.88 | 2019–2025: −1.55 bp/yr, *t* = −1.23 |

The fee gap is **era-robust in the wide ladder** (+10.9 then +10.4) and *strengthens* in
the trio's recent era (SPY's fee has not been cut while its rivals' have). The `winner`
rule is negative in both halves of the ladder.

## Cost sensitivity (winner − cheapest, S&P 500 ETF trio)

| One-way cost | Annual gap | *t* (annual) | *t* (daily HAC) | years positive |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bp (gross) | +2.01 bp/yr | +0.60 | +0.37 | 8/14 |
| 1 bp | +0.33 | +0.10 | +0.03 | 7/14 |
| 5 bp | −6.39 | −1.77 | −1.23 | 3/14 |
| 10 bp | −14.79 | −3.35 | −2.20 | 3/14 |
| 25 bp | −39.98 | −4.92 | −2.98 | 2/14 |

The `winner` rule is a coin flip gross and reliably *negative* at any cost a real switch
actually incurs. The `cheapest` rule has zero turnover, so its gap is cost-invariant.

## The tax caveat — an ASSUMPTION sweep, not a measurement

Years of the published 6.45 bp/yr SPY→VOO fee gap needed to repay the capital-gains tax on
switching an appreciated holding:

| Embedded gain | 0% (sheltered) | 15% | 20% | 23.8% |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| +10% | 0 | 23 | 31 | 37 |
| +25% | 0 | 58 | 78 | 92 |
| +50% | 0 | 116 | **155** | 185 |
| +100% | 0 | 233 | 310 | 369 |

Neither number is on the tape; the grid makes the arithmetic explicit. In a **tax-sheltered**
account the switch is free and the gap is pure gain. In a taxable account with a +50%
embedded gain at 20%, the switch takes **155 years** to repay — the fee gap is real and
utterly unable to justify moving an existing position.

## Cross-checks and honesty notes

- **Hindsight in the selection, quantified above.** The only look-ahead in the study is the
  fee sheet the `cheapest` arm reads; removing it halves the gap (+10.64 → +5.21 bp/yr) but
  does not change its sign, and the *t* survives at +2.68. The persistence result — the
  study's actual headline — uses no fee information at all and is unaffected.
- **Survivorship.** All eight vehicles are survivors, chosen today because they exist today.
  Funds that tracked these indices badly enough to be closed or merged are absent by
  construction, so the *dispersion* of tracking difference is understated and the fee-ladder
  result is measured on the friendliest possible sample. This is named on the Signal axis.
- **NAV-priced legs.** VFIAX, FXAIX and SWPPX are mutual funds: no bid-ask spread, no
  premium/discount, and no intraday switching. They widen the fee ladder to 1.5–9.45 bp,
  which is the only reason the ladder is resolvable at all — but a switch between them
  settles at the next NAV strike, which the cost sweep covers and the tax grid does not
  excuse.
- **Synthetic control** (machinery proof only, never supports the stamp; 8 seeds each): on a
  *planted* 30 bp fee ladder with an 8 bp noise floor, mean year-over-year Spearman is
  **+0.725** (range +0.415 to +0.877) and cheapest − leader is **+35.7 bp/yr**
  (*t* = +10.5); on the flat-fee null the same pipeline returns **−0.079** (range −0.369 to
  +0.138) and **−0.29 bp/yr** (*t* = −0.16). The detector fires when a fee ladder is there
  and stays quiet when it is not.

## Verdict

- **Signal — Mixed.** The claim as posed — that last calendar year's tracking-difference
  rank predicts next year's — **fails where it would be useful**: among near-identical S&P
  500 ETFs the year-over-year Spearman is +0.071 (*t* = +0.43, permutation *p* = 0.96),
  because a 6.45 bp fee spread cannot be resolved through a 10.7 bp measurement floor. What
  *is* real is the thing underneath: across the wider ladder the cheapest fund beats the
  flagship by **+10.64 bp/yr (*t* = +4.85, HAC +4.78, 11/13 years, era-robust)** — halving to
  **+5.21 bp/yr (*t* = +2.68)** once the ex-post fee-sheet pick is removed — and QQQM beats
  QQQ by **+8.55 bp/yr (*t* = +3.95) in 5/5 years**, +8.79 (*t* = +2.93) over the four years
  a rule could have traded it. But the permutation test shows this is a
  *time-invariant level*, not a memory — the all-pairs rank correlation (+0.195) matches the
  consecutive-pair one (+0.253). Half the claim is right, for a reason that makes the other
  half useless: TD ranks persist exactly insofar as expense ratios are published in advance.
  Survivorship flatters the sample, and half the fee-gap magnitude is fee-sheet hindsight.
- **Tradability — Fragile.** The bankable version is not a strategy but a purchase decision:
  buy the cheapest share class and never trade it, worth +3 to +9 bp/yr with zero turnover
  (the +10.64 headline needs a fee sheet from the future; +5.21 is what an investor standing
  at the start of the sample could have had).
  The rotation version delivers **+0.33 bp/yr (*t* = +0.10)** for 10 fund changes in 14
  years, is negative at any cost above 1 bp, and −6.08 bp/yr on the ladder where it has the
  most to choose from. And the gap is far too thin to move an existing taxable holding: a
  +50% embedded gain at 20% takes 155 years to repay. Free at the point of purchase, worth
  nothing thereafter.
